reason: The sources support a surprising and accurate short on the Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall with ample verified claims.
story: Deep in the night sky lies the Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, a titanic structure of galaxies stretching an astonishing ten billion light-years across. Discovered in 2013 by astronomers analyzing gamma-ray bursts, this cosmic mega-structure spans nearly ten percent of the observable universe. According to standard cosmological models, it shouldn't even exist because the universe is supposed to look smooth and uniform on large scales. Yet, there it sits, defying the laws of physics and challenging everything we know about how the cosmos evolved. Some scientists still debate whether it is a true physical structure or just a statistical illusion in our data, leaving the jury out on whether the biggest thing in the universe is actually real.
angle: A colossal ten-billion-light-year structure that shouldn't exist according to our models of the universe.

claims.claim: The Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall measures approximately 10 billion light-years in length.
It was discovered in November 2013 by István Horváth, Jon Hakkila, and Zsolt Bagoly.
The structure was found by analyzing the distribution of gamma-ray bursts using data from space telescopes like Swift and Fermi.
It spans about 10% of the entire diameter of the observable universe.
The name was coined by Johndric Valdez, a Filipino teenager on Wikipedia.
It challenges the cosmological principle, which states the universe should be homogeneous and isotropic on large scales.
The structure is centered near the border of the constellations Draco and Hercules, spanning across multiple constellations.
Gamma-ray bursts are used as a proxy to map matter because they are extremely luminous and associated with massive star formations.
Some studies argue the structure's existence could be due to statistical biases, observational errors, or incomplete data sets.
The proposed ESA mission THESEUS may be needed to decide the question of its existence conclusively.
The clustering of gamma-ray bursts occurs at redshift ranges between 1.6 and 2.1.
Jon Hakkila stated that he would have thought this structure was too big to exist.

disputed: Whether the structure is a genuine physical galaxy filament or merely an artifact of statistical sampling biases and instrument viewing limitations; scripts should attribute this as a matter of ongoing scientific debate.
